why_how.text: Pass only when the maneuver will not interfere with oncoming traffic or the vehicle being overtaken.

Passing signs and pavement markings identify prohibited or unsafe locations, but the driver must still determine whether a pass is safe.

On a two-lane two-way road, passing on the right is allowed only when the vehicle ahead signals a left turn and the move is safe without leaving the roadway.
On a one-way or multilane street with at least two lanes in the driver's direction, passing on the right is allowed only if safe and without leaving the roadway.
Before moving left to pass, check mirrors and blind spots for another vehicle that may already be trying to pass.
Signal left before moving into the left lane to pass.
After overtaking, wait until the passed vehicle appears in the rear-view mirror, then signal right before returning to the right lane.
Use the horn if the vehicle being passed starts drifting toward the passing vehicle.
Finish a pass before reaching a point within two hundred feet of oncoming traffic.
Complete a pass before entering a No Passing zone identified by signs or pavement markings.

why_how.text: Do not join a funeral procession or drive between its vehicles unless a police officer authorizes it.
On a multilane highway, do not pass a funeral procession in the right lane unless the procession occupies the farthest-left lane.
Do not enter an intersection across a funeral procession's path while it is passing through, regardless of the traffic signal's color.
Give funeral processions the right of way.
Every funeral-procession vehicle must use its headlights and taillights.
The first and last vehicles in a funeral procession must also flash warning lights to mark its endpoints.
A vehicle below normal traffic speed that delays at least three vehicles in a rural area or on a two-lane highway must pull off wherever safe to let them pass.

A vehicle designed for no more than twenty-five miles an hour may use public highways only from thirty minutes before sunrise to thirty minutes after sunset, except snow-removal or farm equipment on non-interstate highways with flashing lights visible for five hundred feet.
Slow-moving vehicles must have a foot brake and turn signals and display the approved slow-vehicle emblem.

why_how.text: Tailgating means following too closely and is a common cause of crashes.
When following another car, leave enough space to stop when needed.
Keep the brakes in good working condition when relying on a following gap.
Know the brakes' stopping performance in different conditions and test them often, especially on wet, icy or snowy roads.
The handbook's minimum recommended following interval is three seconds, with more distance needed at high speeds or in bad weather.
For the recommended following-gap check, select a stationary reference ahead of the lead vehicle, such as a tree or roadside sign.
Begin counting three seconds when the vehicle ahead passes the chosen object.
In the handbook's reference-object check, the interval before reaching the object should be at least three seconds and several times longer in bad weather.
Maintain space around the vehicle on all sides to provide time to react to danger.
Stay near the center of the lane and leave enough space ahead to stop or pass safely.
If another vehicle follows too closely, slow down and allow it to pass.
